items.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    The terrestrial sediment archives of northern Germany provide important insights into Late Pleistocene climate variability, but continuous and well‐dated records remain rare. In particular, the age and stratigraphic position of the Oerel and Glinde interstadials within the Early Weichselian to pleniglacial transition remain poorly constrained. These interstadials are commonly attributed to MIS 3, but this assignment is uncertain due to limited numerical dating, reliance on biostratigraphic correlation and the limitations of radiocarbon dating near its upper range. This study presents a new, high‐resolution multi‐proxy record (sedimentology, geochemistry, palynology) from two sediment cores at Lichtenberg, Lower Saxony, positioned directly next to a multi‐phased Middle Palaeolithic archaeological site and supported by a robust chronology based on new optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) ages. The record documents the vegetation and landscape dynamics from the late Eemian interglacial into the Weichselian pleniglacial, capturing major climatic transitions and the onset of cold, periglacial conditions. Within this sequence, we identify two previously unresolved climatic oscillations (Dangenstorf I and II), characterised by expansions of
                    <jats:italic>Betula nana</jats:italic>
                    ‐shrub tundra and increased organic accumulation. Based on pollen assemblages and OSL dating, these oscillations are correlated with the Oerel and Glinde interstadials, which are themselves stratigraphically positioned between the Odderade interstadial and the onset of the Weichselian pleniglacial. Furthermore, our OSL chronology places them firmly within the MIS 5a/4 transition. We assign them to the Greenland interstadials (GI) 20 and 19.2, respectively, rather than to MIS 3 as previously assumed. The Lichtenberg record thus provides a continuous, well‐dated archive that redefines the chronostratigraphy of the Early Weichselian to pleniglacial transition in northern Germany and strengthens its correlation with North Atlantic climate variability.
                  </jats:p>

items.abstract: Prototype-based networks provide inherently interpretable classification by linking predictions to learned exemplars, but their use in 3D point clouds and clinical surface-pair reasoning remains limited. We introduce ProtoPointNet, a prototype-based model for dental occlusion classification from registered upper--lower intraoral arch pairs. Each point is encoded by a 14-dimensional descriptor combining local surface geometry, curvature, and explicit inter-arch displacement and clearance, exposing occlusal relationships to prototype matching. A shared multi-task point-cloud backbone learns axis-specific prototype heads for sagittal-left, sagittal-right, vertical, transverse, and midline classification. To support limited clinical data, we train prototypes from scratch using auxiliary supervision and encoder-freeze hand-off. On Bits2Bites, ProtoPointNet achieves mean test macro-F1 of 0.724 and AUROC of 0.825, with strongest performance on vertical (F1 0.828) and sagittal-left classification (F1 0.807). Projected prototype activations localise to anatomically plausible regions, including posterior molars and premolars for cross-bite evidence and anterior incisors for bite-depth evidence. These results support prototype-based reasoning as a transparent, spatially grounded alternative to black-box 3D classifiers for dental surface-pair analysis.

items.abstract: <jats:p>Ancient pathogen genomics and palaeoproteomics have transformed archaeological research on infectious disease by enabling the detection of pathogens, reconstruction of extinct lineages, and investigation of host responses in past populations. Yet pathogen identification alone addresses only part of retrospective diagnosis: whether an individual experienced disease, which tissues were affected, and how infection contributed to morbidity or death. Palaeoproteomics extends this enquiry through the recovery of pathogen proteins, host immune proteins, and tissue-associated molecules from ancient human remains and associated materials. This review evaluates its diagnostic contribution within the broader reconstruction of ancient disease ecology. Dental calculus provides a particularly rich record of oral host–microbe interactions, combining microbial signals with inflammatory and dietary proteins. Studies of mummified skin, muscle and other soft tissues, dental pulp, skeletal lesions, historical bloodstains, coprolites, and latrine residues further extend the range of evidence available for retrospective diagnosis. Protein-based investigations of intestinal infection also illustrate the need to distinguish antibody-based antigen detection from sequence-based proteomics. Published studies support several levels of inference, ranging from tissue identification and inflammatory processes to specific infection and, more cautiously, clinical disease. They also reveal continuing challenges involving peptide specificity, contamination, source attribution, and the interpretation of disease-associated proteins. Retrospective diagnosis is strongest when molecular findings are consistent with anatomical, archaeological, and historical evidence and help discriminate among plausible alternative diagnoses. Protein evidence therefore contributes not only to individual palaeopathological diagnosis but also to broader reconstructions of relationships among infection, diet, sanitation, care, and social conditions. Future progress will depend on comparative samples with and without independently supported pathological evidence, archaeological validation of diagnostic markers, transparent reporting, broader regional coverage, and sampling of finite human remains.</jats:p>

items.title: Reconstructing ancient disease ecology through pathogen genomics and palaeoproteomics

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Humans routinely keep souvenirs objects retained for the memories they evoke, yet the evolutionary and cognitive consequences of mnemonic collecting remain unclear. Existing discussions of curated objects concentrate on later prehistory and modern humans and view such objects at the social level, as carriers of shared cultural meaning or as markers of status. Here, we address an earlier time period and locate the phenomenon at the personal rather than the social level. By integrating archaeology with theories of extended memory and niche construction, we synthesize evidence consistent with systematic curation of items beyond purely utilitarian needs from the terminal Lower Palaeolithic (~500 kya) onward, including transported distinctive stones, fossils, and the prolonged retention of patinated “old” stone tools whose earlier surfaces were deliberately preserved. We propose that curated keepsakes functioned as portable external memory devices. Beyond cueing recall, they may have helped authenticate self‐relevant past events by providing durable material traces that support source monitoring—distinguishing experienced from imagined events. As such practices became routine, they could have created a “souvenir niche” in which individuals who better integrated internal recollection with external tokens gained fitness benefits. The token's reference is personal, but its consequences can be social, supporting tasks like tracking alliances, reciprocity, and place‐based obligations. These benefits may have strengthened selection on neural systems facilitating the development of autobiographical memory and sense of self via gene–culture coevolution. We outline archaeological, developmental, and experimental predictions that distinguish this mnemonic‐authentication account from aesthetic or economic explanations and suggest approaches for testing them. Viewing curated objects as memory technology links early material culture to the evolutionary shaping of human autobiographical memory.</jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Ontogenetic change is a major source of phenotypic variation among members of a species and is often of greater magnitude than the anatomical differences that distinguish closely related species. Ontogeny has therefore become a problematic confounding variable in vertebrate paleontology, especially in study systems distant from extant crown clades, rendering taxonomic hypothesis testing (a fundamental process in evolutionary biology) rife with difficulty. Paleontologists have adopted quantitative methods to compensate for the perception that juvenile specimens lack diagnostic apomorphies seen in their adult conspecifics. Here, I critically evaluate these methods and the assumptions that guide their interpretation using a μCT dataset comprising growth series of American and Chinese alligator. I find that several widespread assumptions are scientifically unjustifiable and that two popular methods—geometric morphometrics and cladistic analysis of ontogeny—have unacceptably high rates of type II error and present numerous procedural difficulties. However, I also identify a suite of ontogenetically invariant characters that differentiate the living species of
                    <jats:italic>Alligator</jats:italic>
                    throughout ontogeny. These characters overwhelmingly correspond to anatomical systems that develop before (and play a signaling role in) the development of the cranial skeleton itself, suggesting that their ontogenetic invariance is a consequence of the widely conserved vertebrate developmental program. These observations suggest that the architecture of the cranium is fixed early in embryonic development and that ontogenetic remodeling does not alter the topological relationships of the cranial bones or the soft tissue structures they house. I propose a general model for future taxonomic hypothesis tests in the fossil record, in which the hypothesis that two specimens are different ontogenetic stages of a single species can be falsified by the discovery of character differences that cannot be attributed plausibly to ontogenetic variation.
                  </jats:p>
